Divisive

dih-VY-siv — stress on VY · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Divisive describes something that causes strong disagreement and splits people into opposing sides.

The proposal to shorten summer break proved divisive, splitting the town in half.

Worked Example

The decision to remove the school's oldest oak tree became divisive—parents who wanted modernization clashed daily with heritage preservationists who refused to compromise.

Divisive captures not just disagreement but the splitting effect. Unlike 'controversial,' which means people have strong opinions, divisive emphasizes that the issue breaks the community into opposing camps that can't find common ground.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

disagreeable: Disagreeable means unpleasant to deal with - a disagreeable smell, a disagreeable neighbor who complains about everything. It measures how nasty something is to be around, not what it does to a group. Divisive is about the group: a divisive issue splits people into opposing camps. A remark can be disagreeable without dividing anyone.

polarizing: Polarizing means pushing people toward two opposite extremes, hollowing out the middle ground until everyone stands at one pole or the other. Divisive is the broader splitting word: a divisive issue breaks a group into opposing camps of any shape. Polarizing names the specific two-extremes pattern; divisive covers any split.

alienating: Alienating describes what pushes people away - a tone, rule, or decision that makes someone feel unwelcome and cut off, one person at a time. Divisive splits a group into opposing camps that stay and fight. An alienating rule drives members away; a divisive one turns those who remain against each other.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

unifying: bringing people together in shared agreement

conciliatory: meant to calm anger and restore peace

Where it sits · how sharply it splits people apart — debatable → controversial → contentious → divisive

debatable vs. divisive: Debatable is much weaker than divisive: a debatable claim simply invites discussion, while a divisive one splits people into opposing camps.

controversial vs. divisive: Controversial is weaker than divisive on this scale: a controversial plan draws strong opinions on both sides, while a divisive one goes further and breaks the group into camps that stop talking to each other.

contentious vs. divisive: Contentious comes close to divisive but stops short: a contentious topic sparks heated argument, while a divisive one actually breaks a group into rival factions.

Build the Word

The pieces

Root — divis

Root — divis: to divide, separate (Latin dividere) (Latin)

Suffix — -ive

Suffix — -ive: tending to; having the quality of (Latin)

Put it together

Put it together: The root divis- means 'to divide or separate,' and -ive means 'tending to' — so something divisive literally 'tends to divide,' splitting people into opposing sides.

Use the root in a new word: division

Use the root in a new word: division: When a coach splits players into two squads, she makes a division — the same Latin root divis-, 'to separate,' that makes a divisive issue one that separates people into opposing sides.

Word Choice

formal

Divisive is stronger than plain disagreement or even controversial. Use divisive when an issue doesn't just spark debate—it actively fractures a group into opposing camps. For softer disagreement, controversial or debatable is often the better choice.
